items.title: Welcome!
items.text:
Welcome to vulnbrocards.com, home of the "vulnerability brocard."

See How to use for how to apply vulnerability brocards during security triage, and the Brocards themselves for the full list.

items.title: What is a vulnerability brocard?
items.text:
Tip

See the original blog post for more context.

A vulnerability brocard is an aphorism or concise maxim that can help you analyze the correctness and importance of a software vulnerability report when performing triage.

Vulnerability brocards take their name from legal brocards.

Brocards are useful (both in law and in vulnerability triage) because they can be used to preclude the re-litigation of arguments or well-trodden fundamentals.

Example

Many legal system have a de minimis principle, which precludes legal considerations of trivia or "trifling" matters.

For example, New York has a "trivial defect" standard that is used to evaluate trip-and-fall lawsuits. A judge can use this standard to evaluate the evidence and issue a summary judgement if appropriate, potentially avoiding a lengthy and expensive trial process.

In the same way, vulnerability brocards can help us issue "summary judgments" during vulnerability triage.

Read on to see how you can use vulnerability brocards.

items.title: How to use vulnerability brocards
items.text:
Vulnerability brocards are meant to help you make a quick, initial evaluation of a vulnerability report.

They can help you save your time, energy, and sanity by not having to re-litigate each report from first principles.

They can help you decide whether or not to continue triaging the report, or whether you can safely close it. For example, inter alia, a vulnerability brocard might help you triage a report as:

  • Out of scope ("that's something another tool should do")
  • Intended behavior ("we document it as working that way")
  • A non-security bug ("that's broken, but it doesn't need a CVE")

The correct way to use vulnerability brocards is to evaluate the submitted evidence against them: you should take the claims provided by the reporter, and see if they run afoul of one or more brocards.

If they do, you can probably close the report without further triage, saving yourself from needing to analyze the report from first principles.

items.title: Practical use
items.text:
The above is very abstract. Here's a practical example of applying a vulnerability brocard, using Alice (a vulnerability triager) and Bob (a vulnerability reporter):

Bob: I found a vulnerability in LibreWidgets v1.2.3. I can make a user who has LibreWidgets installed run arbitrary code controlled by an attacker.

Alice: What is the mechanism that results in arbitrary code execution?

Bob: LibreWidgets loads configuration from the user's home directory via a file named config.py. If the attacker can write Python into that file, they can run arbitrary code.

Alice: Yes, our configuration is currently defined as a Python script, which means that it runs arbitrary code by design. Please see our docs for an explanation of how that works and VB005 for why that means we don't consider that a report-worthy security concern. Did your report have something in mind besides that?

Bob: No, that's what I had in mind.

Alice: Okay, we're going to close this report as out-of-scope then.

items.title: How not to use vulnerability brocards
items.text:
It's important to only use vulnerability brocards for triage, not as categorical or universal truths.

Vulnerability reporting and triage involves human (and/or LLM) communication, which can be imprecise. Good-faith reporters should be allowed to explain why a brocard might not apply to their report, rather than having the report summarily dismissed after an initial evaluation.

items.title: A note on audience
items.text:
The primary intended audience of this website is people doing open source vulnerability triage.

With that, let's take a look at the brocards.

items.title: Brocards
items.text:
Each individual page here covers a different vulnerability brocard. Each brocard also has a unique VB<NNN> identifier for quick referencing.

As an index:

  • VB001: No vulnerability report without a threat model
  • VB002: No exploit from the heavens
  • VB003: No vulnerability outside of usage
  • VB004: No vulnerability from standard behavior
  • VB005: No vulnerability from documented behavior
  • VB006: No cure worse than the disease
  • VB007: The report is neither necessary nor sufficient

items.title: VB001: No vulnerability report without a threat model
items.text: A vulnerability report can be safely dismissed if it lacks a threat model, or if the threat model presented is incoherent.
path: VB001: No vulnerability report without a threat model

items.title: Examples
items.text:
• A report for a Python API that raises an exception in some undocumented or surprising cases, but doesn’t explain how an attacker could exploit that behavior to cause harm.

  • A report for a hang or stall in a local developer tool. Hangs are undesirable behavior, but the opportunity for harm from one is negligible in a developer tooling context: the developer can always just kill the process.
path: VB001: No vulnerability report without a threat model

items.title: Resources
items.text: • Alex Gaynor: Motion to Dismiss for Failure to State a Vulnerability
path: VB001: No vulnerability report without a threat model

items.title: Nuances
items.text: Not all projects have a documented threat model, or one is that is easy to deduce.
path: VB001: No vulnerability report without a threat model

items.title: VB002: No exploit from the heavens
items.text:
A vulnerability report can be safely dismissed if it describes a severe end state, but only under attacker capability assumptions that are more powerful than the vulnerability itself.

Alternatively: a vulnerability report can be safely dismissed if it implies that the attacker is already more powerful than the attack's outcome would grant.
path: VB002: No exploit from the heavens

items.title: Examples
items.text:
• A report for content manipulation on a web service, where the manipulation can only occur if the attacker is an active meddler in the middle. No vulnerability exists here, because an active MiTM could send entirely arbitrary content, and would not have to limit themselves to manipulating pre-existing content.

  • A report for code execution via memory corruption in CPython, where the memory corruption occurs by directly manipulating CPython's object internals at runtime (via ctypes, for example). No vulnerability exists here, because the attacker is already running arbitrary code to perform the corruption.
path: VB002: No exploit from the heavens

items.title: Resources
items.text: • Raymond Chen: It rather involved being on the other side of this airtight hatchway
path: VB002: No exploit from the heavens

items.title: VB003: No vulnerability outside of usage
items.text: A vulnerability report can be safely dismissed if it describes a behavior that could occur, but does not in fact occur in actual usage of the software.
path: VB003: No vulnerability outside of usage

items.title: Examples
items.text:
• Vulnerabilities in private APIs, where all usages of that API are demonstrably not affected.

  • Re-reports of vulnerabilities in dependencies, where all downstream usage of the dependency is demonstrably not affected by the upstream vulnerability.
path: VB003: No vulnerability outside of usage

items.title: VB004: No vulnerability from standard behavior
items.text:
A vulnerability report can be safely dismissed if the behavior described is a direct consequence of the software’s correct adherence to a standard or specification.

In these instances the vulnerability (if one exists) is present within the standard itself, and not the implementation.
path: VB004: No vulnerability from standard behavior

items.title: Examples
items.text:
• Many standards (inadvisedly) require implementors to accept invalid inputs under the so-called robustness principle. Behavior that adheres to these requirements is not vulnerable per se.

  • Behavior stemming from cryptographic requirements that are insecure in isolation but secure by construction. For example, MD5 is considered an insecure digest but is not insecure when used in an HMAC-MD5 construction.
path: VB004: No vulnerability from standard behavior

items.title: Nuances
items.text: An implementation that chooses to be more strict than the standard requires should be considered vulnerable if the intended strictness is violated.
path: VB004: No vulnerability from standard behavior

items.title: VB005: No vulnerability from documented behavior
items.text: A vulnerability report can be safely dismissed if the behavior is documented to occur, particularly when the documentation explicitly describes the security implications of the behavior or specific contexts in which the software is unsafe to use.
path: VB005: No vulnerability from documented behavior

items.title: Examples
items.text:
• Python's http.server is explicitly documented as not suitable for production use, as it only implements basic security checks.

  • Python's pickle is explicitly documented as not secure, full stop.
path: VB005: No vulnerability from documented behavior

items.title: Nuances
items.text:
A downstream usage that violates the documented guidelines for use may be considered vulnerable.

For example: a report against pickle itself (for e.g. enabling code execution) may be safely dismissed, but a report against a downstream usage of pickle that ignores the documented warnings may be considered valid.
path: VB005: No vulnerability from documented behavior

items.title: Credit
items.text: Suggested by Hugo van Kemenade.
path: VB005: No vulnerability from documented behavior

items.title: VB006: No cure worse than the disease
items.text: A vulnerability report can be safely dismissed if the consequences of addressing it are worse than the consequences of the vulnerability itself.
path: VB006: No cure worse than the disease

items.title: Examples
items.text: • Most ReDoS "vulnerabilities" require significantly more maintainer effort and attention to triage than their threat/risk actually warrants.
path: VB006: No cure worse than the disease

items.title: Resources
items.text: • ReDoS "vulnerabilities" and misaligned incentives
path: VB006: No cure worse than the disease

items.title: VB007: The report is neither necessary nor sufficient
items.text:
The presence of a vulnerability report (and a CVE or other identifier for that report) is neither necessary nor sufficient for a vulnerability to exist.

This is true in both directions:

  • Many vulnerabilities are never formally reported.
  • Many formal reports do not describe meaningful vulnerabilities.

Consequently, no unvalidated assumption should ever be made about the relationship between the presence of a report and the presence of a vulnerability.
path: VB007: The report is neither necessary nor sufficient

items.title: Examples
items.text: • A vulnerability report based on a CVE for an upstream component where the affected surfaces are used, but the upstream CVE is not a meaningful vulnerability.
path: VB007: The report is neither necessary nor sufficient
